hints: Think of Kstab as the equilibrium constant for forming the complex from the hexaaqua copper(II) ion and free ammonia ligands.
walkthrough:
Picture the formation equilibrium**
Start from the aqua ion in solution. Copper(II) exists as $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ and ammonia ligands replace water to give $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$. So the balanced formation step is $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + 4NH_3 \rightleftharpoons [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+} + 6H_2O$.

Write the Kstab expression**
$K_{stab}$ is products over reactants, omitting water because it is the solvent in large excess. That gives $$K_{stab} = \frac{[[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}]}{[[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}][NH_3]^4}$$ Remember the power 4 comes from the four $NH_3$ ligands.

hints: Recall the very distinctive colour seen when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
walkthrough:
Link the reagent to the observation**
When excess aqueous ammonia is added to pale blue $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$, the ligands are exchanged to form $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$. This tetraammine complex has a famous intense colour that is quite different from the pale blue starting solution, a deep dark blue.
Final answer: Deep (dark / royal) blue solution.

hints: Heating drives off $NH_3$, so water molecules can act as a base to remove protons and leave $Cu(OH)_2$ plus ammonium ions.
walkthrough:
See why heating destroys the complex**
Gentle heating expels dissolved $NH_3$ gas from solution. Loss of ligand destabilises $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ and water now attacks the copper centre.

Balance the hydrolysis to the hydroxide**
Water provides $OH^-$ for the $Cu(OH)_2$ precipitate and $H^+$ which is captured by $NH_3$ to make $NH_4^+$. Balancing Cu, N, H and O and charge gives $$[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+} + 2H_2O \rightarrow Cu(OH)_2 + 2NH_4^+ + 2NH_3$$

hints: Concentrated HCl provides a very high concentration of $Cl^-$ ligands, so a chloro complex of copper(II) forms.
Recall the formula and charge of the copper chloro complex formed in concentrated HCl and balance $Cu(OH)_2$ with $H^+$ and $Cl^-$ to make water.
walkthrough:
Identify complex Y**
With concentrated HCl, $Cl^-$ is in huge excess and replaces all O donor ligands to give the tetrachlorocuprate(II) ion, $[CuCl_4]^{2-}$. That is Y.

Build the balanced equation**
$Cu(OH)_2$ is a base, so $H^+$ from the acid neutralises $OH^-$ to water, while $Cl^-$ coordinates. Balancing gives $$Cu(OH)_2 + 4HCl \rightarrow [CuCl_4]^{2-} + 2H_2O + 2H^+$$ Check: Cu 1 to 1, Cl 4 to 4, O 2 to 2, H 6 to 6, charge 0 to 0.

hints: Think of the familiar colour of the chloro complex in concentrated HCl versus the familiar colour of copper(II) sulfate solution.
Recall that 4 coordinate $Cu(II)$ chloro complex is tetrahedral while the 6 coordinate aqua ion is octahedral.
walkthrough:
Assign Y from part (c)**
Y is $[CuCl_4]^{2-}$. It is yellow and with coordination number 4 it adopts a tetrahedral geometry.

Assign Z from dilute sulfuric acid**
Dilute $H_2SO_4$ simply dissolves $Cu(OH)_2$ as an acid base reaction to reform the hexaaqua ion. Sulfate is not a strong ligand here, so Z is $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$, which is blue (pale blue) and octahedral with coordination number 6.
Final answer: Y: colour = yellow, geometry = tetrahedral. Z: colour = blue / pale blue, geometry = octahedral, formula = $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$.

hints: Start by remembering what happens to the five d orbitals when ligands approach the $Cu^{2+}$ ion.
Think about what must happen for visible light to interact with those split d orbitals.
Consider what happens to a d electron when it absorbs the correct photon.
Relate the colour you see to the colour that was removed by absorption.
Compare the ligands in Y ($Cl^-$) and Z ($H_2O$) and how different ligands change the size of the d orbital energy gap.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
In a free $Cu^{2+}$ ion the five 3d orbitals have the same energy. When ligands ($Cl^-$ or $H_2O$) approach, they repel d electrons unequally, so the d set splits into two levels with an energy gap $\Delta E$. $Cu(II)$ is $d^9$, so there is a vacancy to allow promotion.

Absorb light to promote an electron**
If a photon has energy $h\nu$ exactly equal to $\Delta E$, it is absorbed and a lower level d electron is excited to the upper level. This is a d-d transition.

See the complementary colour**
The solution transmits all the colours that were not absorbed. Your eye sees the mixture of transmitted light, which is the complementary colour of the absorbed light.

Explain why Y and Z differ**
$Cl^-$ and $H_2O$ are different ligands with different field strengths, so they split the d orbitals by different amounts. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed ($\Delta E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$), so the complementary colour transmitted is different. Hence yellow for $[CuCl_4]^{2-}$ and blue for $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d orbitals to split into two sets of different energy.
Light of a specific wavelength / frequency is absorbed, promoting / exciting a d electron to the higher set.
Colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed.
$\Delta E$ is different for Y and Z because ligands are different, so different frequency / wavelength absorbed, giving different colours.
